message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
## Verdict

The price increases are reasonable and probably worth doing. But the paper's two headline claims don't hold as written:

1. **The mushroom risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu (80%), not the weakest.** Replacing it with a special at the specials' typical 64% margin would *lose* about £200 a week.
2. **The £42,000 a year ignores the 12% beef price rise the paper itself reports,** and possibly VAT. A realistic figure is roughly **£20,000–£35,000 a year**, depending on VAT treatment, and still assuming volumes hold.

Recommendation 5.2 should be dropped, and the projection restated.

## What's right

- **Table 1 is internally consistent.** Every margin matches its price and cost, and the plates sum to 1,050.
- **The £810 arithmetic is correct.** £1 × 310 + £1 × 260 + £2 × 120 = £810 a week, or £42,120 a year.
- **All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints:** fish £17.98, burger £16.50, steak £29.50.
- **The ~71% margin calculation reproduces,** before the beef rise. I estimate the current main-course margin at about 69–70%, rising to about 70.8%.
- **Pricing has been frozen since September 2024 while costs rose,** so an increase is overdue.

## 1. The risotto is the most profitable dish per sale

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate | Weekly gross profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** | £11.20 | £1,008 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 | £3,534 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 | £2,808 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 | £1,962 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 | £1,872 |

Its percentage margin is the best on the menu. Its profit per plate beats both the burger and the curry. It also isn't uniquely the lowest seller: specials sell the same 90 plates a week.

**If the replacement special performs like current specials (64%) at £14**, each plate earns £8.96 instead of £11.20. That costs **about £200 a week, or £10,500 a year**. It may also lose diners who come for a vegetarian main they know.

**Suggestion:** keep the risotto. If anything, it's a candidate for promoting more prominently.

## 2. The beef cost rise isn't netted off

From 1 April, beef rises 12%, the same day the new prices start. Most of the steak's £10.40 food cost is beef, and part of the burger's £4.20:

- **Steak:** about +£1.25 a plate. That cuts the £2 increase to roughly **+£0.75**, which is £90 a week, not £240.
- **Burger:** about +£0.25–0.50 a plate, depending on how much of the cost is beef. That is £60–130 a week.

Together this removes roughly **£210–280 a week** from the projected gain. It also pulls the main-course margin back to about **69–70%, not 71%**.

## 3. Check whether the margins include VAT

UK menu prices include 20% VAT, and the table's margins appear to be calculated on menu prices. If so:

- **Only 83p of each £1 increase is revenue.** The £810 becomes **£675 a week**.
- **Every margin in the table is overstated.** For example, fish and chips is about 63% on its VAT-exclusive price, not 69%. The paper should say which basis it uses, and stick to it for the 70% target.

## Corrected projection

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| As stated | £810 | £42,100 |
| Less beef cost rise | ~£530–600 | ~£28,000–31,000 |
| Also net of VAT (if margins include it) | ~£400–465 | **~£21,000–24,000** |
| If risotto replaced at 64% margin | −£200 more | −£10,500 more |

Annual figures assume 52 trading weeks; adjust for any closures.

## 4. "Volumes hold" is untested, so give the break-even

The paper assumes no customers are lost. The more useful figure for the owners is the **break-even volume drop**: how far sales of each dish could fall before the price rise loses money.

| Dish | Profit per plate, before → after | Break-even volume drop |
|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £11.40 → £12.40 | ~8% |
| Burger | £10.80 → ~£11.40* | ~5% |
| Steak | £15.60 → ~£16.35* | ~5% |

*After the beef rise, mid-estimate, on the paper's VAT-inclusive basis.

So the increases still pay off unless volumes fall by more than roughly 5–8%. That's plausible, but it isn't guaranteed.

A few related points:
- **No longer the cheapest.** At the new prices, all three dishes are above the cheapest competitor (£16.95, £15.50 and £27.00). The Copper Kettle would sit mid-pack, not be "the value option".
- **The 2024 evidence is thin.** "No visible effect on bookings" from the 2024 rise needs data behind it.
- **Lunch's share isn't stated.** The paper says lunch trade is price-sensitive but "small". Give the actual share.

## 5. The monitoring would be misleading

Comparing April–May plate counts against January–February will mix the price effect with seasonality. Spring trade is usually stronger than winter, so a real fall in volume could be hidden. Two fixes:

- **Use a seasonal comparison.** Compare against **April–May 2025**, or the same weeks last year.
- **Set a trigger in advance.** For example, if any dish falls more than 8% below the seasonal comparison, review its price.

## Smaller points

- **Trading days.** The Recommendation says "six trading days a week". Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **Scope.** The overall food margin fell from 70% to 67% "across all courses". Starters and desserts aren't reviewed, so mains alone may not restore the target.
- **"We will not draw attention to the increases."** That's a reasonable choice, but with 60% repeat guests, regulars will notice anyway. Brief staff on how to respond.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Drop 5.2 and keep the risotto.**
2. **Restate the projection net of the beef rise,** and on a stated VAT basis. Expect about £21,000–31,000 a year rather than £42,000.
3. **Add the break-even volume table,** so the owners can see the margin for error.
4. **Monitor against the same weeks last year,** with a pre-set trigger for review.
5. **Fix "six trading days".**

The price increases themselves are sensible, and the owners can approve them with confidence once the figures are corrected.
